issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette:
James, a 42-year-old ship captain, still remembers the morning the Meridian Star exploded. He was on the bridge of his own vessel, docking at a port when a nearby cargo ship—later found to be carrying unsecured military-grade explosives—blew apart in a chain of detonations. A deafening bang threw debris across the docks; a chunk of metal struck the bridge window an inch from his face. Coast Guard and port police arrived in full uniform, but their response was disorganized and delayed. The owners of the other ship were never charged, let alone convicted. No one was held accountable. In the months after, James tried not to think about those moments—the hot shockwave, the screaming—because he was certain that if he let the memory surface, it would overwhelm him entirely.

The first sign that something was wrong was his sleep. Even at home, with the house quiet, he couldn’t let himself drift off; he needed to stay alert, listening for any sudden bang. He started choosing the seat at the dinner table with his back to the wall, scanning the room before sitting down. At work, he became hypervigilant toward his own crew, watching for anyone who seemed unpredictable or aggressive. The belief that he could not rely on other people—that they would fail him, that they were potential threats—made every unfamiliar port feel dangerous, so he began avoiding new routes and delegating safety inspections to his first officer, giving up a core responsibility just to stay in known waters where he felt he could assess the risks. He also took up online gambling late at night, using the rush to distract himself from intrusive images of the explosion.

That same belief—that others were untrustworthy and that the people responsible had faced no consequences—sharpened his reaction to triggers. Seeing a police or military uniform now made his pulse race, because authority figures reminded him of the failed response. A crew member tossing a rope coil onto the deck would make him flinch, as if the object were a piece of shrapnel. The louder the bang—a docking horn, a cargo hatch slamming—the more his body braced for the next explosion. And because he was constantly scanning for danger, he saw more of it: a uniformed port official walking toward him felt like an accusation, a worker throwing a line felt like an attack.

The strategies he had adopted to manage the threat only deepened his negative appraisals. By dropping important duties, he told himself that he could not trust anyone else to handle them properly, reinforcing the idea that he was alone and that others would let him down. Gambling kept his mind off the memories for a few hours, but afterwards he felt more out of control, more convinced that no one was ever held to account. The cycle tightened: his hypervigilance made him avoid people and places, which made him more isolated, which confirmed that he could not rely on anyone. At home, his wife grew frustrated by his refusal to go to new restaurants or visit friends, and she found the credit card statements showing his gambling losses.

What finally brought James to seek help was a near-miss on the bridge. A junior officer accidentally knocked a heavy tool box off a shelf; the crash sounded like the explosion. James froze, grabbed the railing, and shouted at the man—then realized that his own fear had made him a danger to the crew. He was most afraid that he would never stop seeing the world as a series of possible detonations, and he quietly hoped that talking about it might loosen the grip of a disaster that, for everyone else, was already years in the past.
